name: braised turnips
instructions:
Classic french braised / glazed turnips (navets glacés). Turnips cooked in butter (or ghee) + water + salt until tender, then the liquid reduces to a glossy glaze. Same technique works for other dense roots — RUTABAGA and CELERY ROOT are direct substitutions in the turnip slot.

Same technique family as [[glazed-carrots]] variant A (Julia's butter + sugar + water braise-and-glaze).

SERVES 4. Wide sauté pan or skillet with a lid.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 1/2 lb DENSE ROOT VEGETABLE — turnips (default), rutabaga, or celery root — peeled and cut into wedges or 1-inch chunks
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter OR ghee
- 1/2 tsp salt
- freshly ground black pepper
- water (to about halfway up the roots)
- OPTIONAL: 1/2 tsp sugar (for a more classical navets-glacés-style glossy glaze — see notes)
- OPTIONAL: fresh parsley or chives, chopped, for garnish
- OPTIONAL: squeeze of LEMON or LIME juice at the finish (see LEMON/LIME FINISH note — brightens the glaze, pairs especially well with [[mint-cilantro-skillet]] as a side)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREP: peel roots and cut into even wedges or ~1-inch chunks so they cook at the same rate.

2. ARRANGE IN A WIDE PAN: place roots in a single layer in a wide sauté pan or skillet (don't stack — you want the liquid to reach each piece). Add the butter or ghee (cut into small pieces so it distributes), salt, pepper, and sugar if using.

3. ADD WATER TO HALFWAY UP: pour in enough water to come about HALFWAY UP the roots. Not covering them completely — half-covered is the braise depth.

4. BRAISE COVERED: bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low, cover, and cook 15-20 min until roots are tender through when pierced with a fork. Rutabaga and celery root may take a few minutes longer than turnips (denser).

5. GLAZE — UNCOVER AND REDUCE: uncover the pan, raise the heat to medium-high, and let the remaining liquid reduce down to a syrupy glaze that coats the roots (~5 min). Toss / swirl the pan occasionally so the roots get evenly coated as the liquid reduces.

6. FINISH + SERVE: adjust salt and pepper. Optional: squeeze of lemon or lime juice off heat (see LEMON/LIME FINISH note). Scatter fresh parsley or chives on top if using. Serve warm.
notes:
Classic french glazed turnips — navets glacés. Same technique family as [[glazed-carrots]] variant A (Julia's butter + sugar + water braise-and-glaze); different vegetable in the same slot.

=== DENSE ROOT SWAPS — TURNIPS, RUTABAGA, CELERY ROOT ===

Same technique works for any dense root vegetable, not just turnips:
- TURNIPS (default): the classic navets-glacés vegetable. Slightly sweet, slightly bitter, tender through in the shortest time.
- RUTABAGA (swede): denser and sweeter than turnips; ~5 min longer in the braise. Reads heartier — more meat-substitute-adjacent (see [[lentil-cottage-pie]]'s roots-as-meat-substitute pattern).
- CELERY ROOT (celeriac): most delicate/vegetal of the three. Also takes ~5 min longer than turnips. Reads a bit more herbal-vegetal in the finished glaze.

Mix and match works too — half turnips + half rutabaga is a nice combination if you want both registers. Cut all pieces roughly the same size regardless of which root(s) you use.

=== BUTTER OR GHEE — BOTH WORK ===

Butter is the traditional french choice. GHEE also works cleanly here — same fat function, slightly nuttier and higher smoke point, and it opens the recipe to pairing with indian-adjacent dishes (see [[mint-cilantro-skillet]] pairing note in this file). Both produce the same braised-and-glazed result.

=== LEMON/LIME FINISH (OPTIONAL) — BRIGHTENER + PAIRING BRIDGE ===

A squeeze of LEMON or LIME juice off heat at the finish (after the glaze reduces) brightens the buttery-savory register and prevents the braised roots from reading one-note. Small amount — 1 tsp is enough.

ESPECIALLY GOOD WHEN PAIRING WITH [[mint-cilantro-skillet]] (chicken/tofu) OR [[jaffrey-lentils]] (the split-out madhur-jaffrey tarka dal that shares the same herb pair): the lemon or lime on the turnips echoes the lime in the skillet or the fresh-herb finish in the lentils. Reach for lime specifically when pairing with either; lemon for a more general french-pairing register.

=== BRAISE-AND-GLAZE TECHNIQUE — TWO PHASES ===

The technique has two distinct phases in one pan:
1. BRAISE COVERED: roots cook through in the water + fat liquid, half-covered, low heat, ~15-20 min. This is the tender-through phase.
2. UNCOVER AND GLAZE: raise heat, let the liquid reduce down until it's a syrupy glaze that coats the roots. The butter (or ghee) concentrates as the water boils off, coating the surfaces. If sugar was added, it deepens the glaze into a proper glossy caramel finish (see SUGAR note).

Both phases are load-bearing. Skip the braise and the roots end up undercooked with a burnt glaze. Skip the glaze and the roots are tender but sit in watery liquid — not what the dish is going for.

=== ROOT CHUNK SIZE — EVEN CUTS COOK EVENLY ===

Cut all pieces roughly the same size (wedges or ~1-inch chunks) so they cook through at the same rate. Uneven cuts leave you with some pieces mushy and others still firm at the glaze stage. Peel — the skin is edible but reads bitter/chewy in this format across all three roots.

=== BUTTER OR GHEE, NOT OLIVE OIL ===

This is a butter-forward french technique (or ghee — see BUTTER OR GHEE note above). Olive oil doesn't give you the same glaze character — butter's milk solids caramelize together into the finished glossy coating. Olive oil braise would push toward a mediterranean lathera direction (see [[fasolakia-lathera]] for that register instead).

=== SUGAR IS OPTIONAL — FOR THE CLASSIC NAVETS-GLACÉS GLOSSY GLAZE ===

1/2 tsp sugar is optional. The base recipe (butter/ghee + salt + water) works cleanly on its own — the roots braise through, the fat + concentrated aromatics coat them at the reduction stage, done.

ADDING 1/2 TSP SUGAR pushes the finish toward the more classical navets-glacés glossy glaze — the sugar concentrates in the reduction and gives the roots a proper caramelized coating rather than just a fat glaze. Worth including if you want the traditional french presentation; skip for a simpler / everyday braise.

=== WATER HALF-COVERING — NOT SUBMERGED ===

The liquid should come about halfway up the turnips, not cover them entirely. Submerged turnips boil rather than braise, and you end up with too much water to reduce cleanly into a glaze. Half-covered gives the right balance — enough liquid to braise through, not so much that the glaze step drags on.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[glazed-carrots]]: same braise-and-glaze technique, different vegetable. Variant A there (Julia's butter + sugar + water) is essentially this recipe with carrots swapped for turnips. If you like this, that recipe scales the same way.
- [[marcella-lemon-celery]]: another braised-vegetable-side (Marcella's celery + potatoes + olive oil + lemon), simpler and cleaner than this butter-forward french style. Different register (italian, olive-oil-forward, lemon-brightened).
- [[indian-mashed-eggplant]]: eggplant version of the braised-vegetable-side format — different technique (roasted-then-mashed) but same family (vegetable-forward side dish).
- [[breadcrumb-leeks]]: another french braised-vegetable side (currently a stub — leeks + lemon-pepper breadcrumbs).
- [[dauphinois]]: turnip use-case in a different format (potato-and/or-turnip gratin baked in cream). If you have turnips and want something richer than this braise, that's the other direction.
original_chef: Classic french technique — navets glacés (glazed turnips). Not a specific author; parallel to Julia Child's glazed carrots (see [[glazed-carrots]]).
